overview: The Apinayé, also written Apinajé, are a Jê-speaking Indigenous people of northern Tocantins, in the region between the Araguaia and Tocantins rivers. Their history includes village autonomy, ceremonial associations, mixed gardens, music and skilled work with forest materials. Communities continue to defend their territory and teach knowledge across generations.

periods.title: A woven bag enters a museum collection
periods.summary: A palm-leaflet bag from São José entered the UFG museum in June 1970. The record documents a particular object and its collection history, rather than dating the invention of Apinayé basketry.

periods.title: Territorial recognition with exclusions
periods.summary: Apinayé mobilization and support from other Indigenous peoples helped secure demarcation. The adopted boundary still excluded important land west of the Transamazonian highway.

periods.title: Presidential approval of demarcation
periods.summary: A decree dated 3 November 1997 approved the administrative demarcation of Apinayé Indigenous Land in Tocantins. This was a distinct step in a longer territorial struggle.

periods.title: Family gardens and seed exchange
periods.summary: The PEMPXÀ association supported gardens and circulated seeds obtained through regional farmers and Indigenous seed fairs. Families connected food production with teaching children about cultivation.

periods.title: Singers teach and discuss the future of music
periods.summary: Célio Ribeiro Dias Apinajé documented a gathering at Boi Morto in 2018 and interviewed singers in 2019. Their accounts describe learning through performance and hopes for stronger school support.

periods.title: A nursery and territorial knowledge
periods.summary: A Pyka Mex association project began in 2020 at Prata. Its later report records collective seedling production and expeditions bringing young people together with older knowledge holders.

sections.title: Objects and the skills behind them

items.text: A bag from São José, catalogued as 70.03.012 at the UFG museum, uses woven palm leaflets and a carrying handle. Its function was to store and transport personal belongings. The museum purchased it in 1970 but did not record its maker. It preserves evidence of practical weaving, while leaving an individual craftsperson’s story unknown.

Necklace 91.06.133 combines buriti fiber with differently colored seeds, bamboo sections, quills and green feathers. Its pendant repeats several of those materials. Making such an ornament involved selecting and assembling contrasting textures and colors, not simply finding a single decorative substance. The collection records its entry in 1991, without establishing when it was made or who made it.

A gourd flute, object 79.01.0881, hangs from a cord of plant fibers. The museum acquired it by purchase in 1979. Its dossier mentions a seed pendant that is now missing, a reminder that surviving objects can change after collection. The instrument documents material choices for making sound; its catalogue alone cannot recover the music once played on it.

The ethnographic account describes gardens associated with women’s households, with men clearing vegetation and women participating in planting corn, manioc and other crops. Rice, corn and manioc grow together; later beans can climb the standing corn stalks. This arrangement combines crops with different growth habits and makes a field a sequence of linked tasks.

Villages act as local political communities, with household relationships, leaders and ceremonial groups organizing collective life. Families may establish a new settlement rather than remain permanently within one village. This helps explain why a single outline on a map does not represent a centralized Apinayé kingdom with one ruler over every community.

In a January 2015 statement, the PEMPXÀ association described gardens begun in 2013 and supported again in 2014. Families planted manioc, beans, bananas, corn and rice. Seeds came through exchanges with farmers in the Bico do Papagaio region and fairs held by Kayapó and Krahô peoples, linking household food security with wider relationships.

The association emphasized that children and grandchildren learned planting, seed conservation and care for land and water while joining family garden work. It also reported concern about drought and limited support. Its account presents food production as both skilled labor and education, with future harvests depending on environmental conditions as well as knowledge.

Singer Cleonice Apinagé told researcher Célio Ribeiro Dias Apinajé that she learned by attending celebrations with her mother and listening to singers. She also described women completing parts of a song in collective performance. The account connects musical knowledge with participation and repeated listening, rather than treating a written score as the only route to learning.

Other interviewees described recordings as useful for learning and wanted stronger support for music in schools. At Boi Morto’s 2018 gathering, the researcher observed people singing together indoors by day and in the plaza at night. These discussions show singers actively considering how teaching can adapt while preserving relationships between music, memory and community.

A project led by the Pyka Mex association at Prata reported establishing a nursery and collectively producing about 5,000 seedlings. Women, young people and elders joined seed-collecting expeditions; plants and seeds went to neighboring communities and partners. Territorial visits and conversations with elders connected plant work to knowledge of local history, boundaries and threats.

Fagundes and Barbosa’s archival study identifies nineteenth-century records of Apinayé gardens supplying both local residents and boats on the Tocantins. Those records connect agricultural work with regional exchange. They also explain why excluded fertile lands mattered materially, alongside their significance in community history and relationships with particular places.

The 1985 demarcation followed Indigenous mobilization, but its boundary excluded land west of the Transamazonian highway. A later presidential decree, dated 3 November 1997, formally approved the administrative demarcation. Recognizing this sequence avoids confusing one legal act with the beginning of Apinayé ownership or the resolution of every land claim.

ending.text: Apinayé communities continue through gardens, teaching, associations and territorial action despite restrictions on their land. The map’s interval of 1492 to 1500 is imported coverage; 1500 is not a cultural ending, conquest date or the dissolution of an Apinayé state.
